source_text: Audio poetas quoque « unum patrem divum atque hominum » praedicantes, et « talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem duxerit. » Quid Mantuanus Maro? nonne apertius, proximius, verius? « Principio, ait, coelum et terras, » et caetera mundi membra « spiritus intus alit, et infusa mens agitat. Inde hominum pecudumque genus » et quidquid aliud animalium. Idem alio loco, mentem istam et spiritum, Deum nominat; haec enim vera sunt: Deum namque ire per omnes Terrasque tractusque maris coelumque profundum. Unde homines, et pecudes, unde imber et ignis. Quid aliud et a nobis Deus, quam mens et ratio et spiritus praedicatur? Recenseamus, si placet, disciplinas philosophorum, deprehendes eos, etsi sermonibus variis, ipsis tamen rebus in hanc unam coire et conspirare sententiam. (XII) Omitto illos rudes et veteres qui de suis dictis sapientes esse meruerunt. Sit Thales Milesius omnium primus, qui primus omnium de coelestibus disputavit. Is Milesius Thales rerum initium aquam dixit; Deum autem eam mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formaverit. Eho! altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ab homine potuerit inveniri; a Deo traditum. Vides Philosophi principalis nobiscum penitus opinionem consonare. Anaximenes deinceps, et post Apolloniates Diogenes, aera Deum statuunt, infinitum et immensum. Horum quoque similis de divinitate consensio est. Anaxagorae vero descriptio et motus infinitae mentis Deus dicitur. Et Pythagorae Deus est animus, per universam rerum naturam commeans et intentus: ex quo etiam animalium omnium vita capiatur. Xenophanem notum est omne infinitum cum mente Deum tradere; et Antisthenem, populares deos multos, sed naturalem unum praecipuum; Zeuxippum [ imp. Spensippum], vim naturalem, animalem, qua omnia regantur, Deum nosse. Quid Democritus? quamvis atomorum primus inventor,26 nonne plerumque naturam, quae imagines fundat, et intelligentiam, Deum loquitur? Straton quoque et ipse naturam: etiam Epicurus ille qui deos aut otiosos fingit aut nullos, naturam tamen superponit. Aristoteles variat, et adsignat tamen unam potestatem. Nam interim mentem, mundum interim Deum dicit, interim mundo Deum praeficit. Aristoteles Ponticus variat, alias mundo, alias menti divinae tribuens principatum. Heraclides Ponticus quoque Deo divinam mentem, quamvis varie, adscribit. Theophrastus, et Zenon, et Chrysippus, et Cleanthes, sunt et ipsi multiformes; sed ad unitatem providentiae omnes revolvuntur. Cleanthes enim mentem, modo animum, modo aethera, plerumque rationem Deum disseruit. Zenon, ejusdem magister, naturalem legem atque divinam, et aethera interim, interdumque rationem, vult omnium esse principium. Item interpretando Junonem aera, Jovem coelum, Neptunum mare, ignem esse Vulcanum, et caeteros similiter vulgi deos elementa esse monstrando, publicum arguit graviter et revincit errorem. Eadem fere Chrysippus, vim divinam, rationalem naturam, et mundum interim, et fatalem necessitatem Deum credit, Zenonemque interpretatione physiologiae in Hesiodi, Homeri Orpheique carminibus imitatur. (XIII) Babylonio etiam Diogeni disciplina est exponendi et disserendi Jovis partum et ortum Minervae, et hoc genus caeterarum rerum vocabula esse, non deorum. (XIV) Nam Socraticus Xenophon formam Dei veri negat videri posse, et ideo quaeri non oportere. Aristo Stoicus , comprehendi omnino non posse. Uterque majestatem Dei, intelligendi desperatione; senserunt. Platoni apertior de Deo et rebus ipsis et nominibus oratio est; et quae tota esset coelestis, nisi persuasionis civilis nonnumquam admixtione sordesceret. Platoni itaque in Timaeo Deus est ipso suo nomine mundi parens, artifex animae, coelestium terrenorumque fabricator; quem et invenire difficile, prae nimia et incredibili potestate; et, cum inveneris, in publicum dicere impossibile praefatur. (XV) Eadem fere et ista quae nostra sunt nam et Deum novimus et parentem omnium dicimus, et numquam publice, nisi interrogati, praedicamus.
pass_a_gloss: I hear that poets also preach that there is one Father of gods and men, and that the mind of mortals is such as the Parent of all has deemed it to be. What about the Mantuan Maro? Does he not say it more openly, more closely, more truly? At the beginning, he says, heaven and earth and the other parts of the world are nourished by a spirit within and a mind that has been infused, and from this comes the race of men and beasts and whatever other animals. In another place, he calls this mind and spirit God; for it is true that God goes through all lands and tracts of sea and deep heaven. From Him come men and beasts, from Him come rain and fire. What else do we preach about God, except that He is mind and reason and spirit? Let us review, if you please, the teachings of the philosophers, and you will find that they, although they use different words, nevertheless come together and agree on this one opinion. I pass over those rude and ancient ones who have been considered wise because of their sayings. Let Thales of Miletus be the first of all, who first of all discussed heavenly things. This Thales of Miletus said that the beginning of things is water, but that God is the mind that has formed all things from water. Behold, a reason higher and more sublime than water and spirit, which could not have been discovered by man, but was handed down by God. You see that the principal opinion of the philosophers is in complete agreement with ours. Anaximenes and then Diogenes of Apollonia establish air as God, infinite and immense. The consensus of these men about divinity is similar. Anaxagoras truly calls the description and motion of the infinite mind God. And Pythagoras says that God is the soul that moves through and is intent on the whole nature of things, from which also the life of all animals is derived. It is well known that Xenophanes hands down that all that is infinite is God with a mind, and that Antisthenes says that there are many popular gods, but one natural and principal God; and that Zeuxippus knows God as the natural, animal force by which all things are ruled. What about Democritus? Although he is the first inventor of atoms, does he not often speak of nature, which founds images, and intelligence, as God? Strato also says that nature is God, and even Epicurus, who either imagines gods as idle or as non-existent, nevertheless places nature above them. Aristotle varies, but nevertheless assigns one power; for he sometimes says that the mind is God, sometimes the world, and sometimes he places God over the world. Aristotle of Pontus varies, sometimes attributing the principality to the world, sometimes to the divine mind. Heraclides of Pontus also ascribes the divine mind to God, although in various ways. Theophrastus, and Zeno, and Chrysippus, and Cleanthes, are also multiform, but they all revolve around the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discusses God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as ether, and often as reason. Zeno, his teacher, wants the natural law and the divine law, and sometimes ether, and sometimes reason, to be the principle of all things. Similarly, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, and fire as Vulcan, and showing that the other gods of the people are elements, he seriously accuses and overcomes the public error. Chrysippus is almost the same, believing that the divine power, the rational nature, and the world, and the fatal necessity, are God, and he imitates Zeno in the physiological interpretation of the songs of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus. The Babylonian Diogenes also has a teaching that expounds and discusses the birth and origin of Jupiter and Minerva, and that these and other such things are words, not gods. For the Socratic Xenophon denies that the form of the true God can be seen, and therefore should not be sought. The Stoic Aristo says that it cannot be comprehended at all. Both have felt the majesty of God, and have despaired of understanding it. Plato's speech about God and things and names is more open, and would be entirely heavenly, if it were not sometimes sullied by the admixture of civil persuasion. Therefore, in the Timaeus, God is the Parent of the world, the artisan of the soul, the fabricator of heavenly and earthly things, whom it is difficult to find because of His excessive and incredible power, and who, when found, it is impossible to speak of publicly. We have almost the same things, for we know God and call Him the Parent of all, and we never preach publicly, unless we are asked.

pass_b_english: I hear poets also proclaiming one Father of gods and men, and that the mind of mortals is exactly what the Parent of all has ordained. Take the Mantuan Maro — does he not say it more openly, more directly, more truly? At the beginning, he says, heaven and earth and all the world's members are sustained by an inner spirit, and an infused mind sets them in motion. From this comes the race of men and beasts and every other living thing. Elsewhere he names this mind and spirit God; for it is true that God passes through all lands and tracts of sea and deep heaven. From him come men and beasts; from him come rain and fire. What else do we proclaim about God than that he is mind and reason and spirit? Let us review the philosophers' teachings, if you please, and you will find that, despite their varied language, they converge and agree on this single view.

I pass over those crude ancients who earned a reputation for wisdom from their sayings. Let Thales of Miletus stand first, the first to debate heavenly matters. Thales said water is the origin of things, but God is the mind that formed everything from water. A reason higher and more sublime than water and spirit — one no human could have discovered, but God handed down. You see the philosophers' leading opinion in full accord with ours. Anaximenes and then Diogenes of Apollonia posited air as God, infinite and immense. Their consensus on divinity is similar. Anaxagoras calls the description and motion of infinite mind God. Pythagoras says God is the soul that pervades and attends the whole nature of things, from which the life of all animals also springs. It is well known that Xenophanes teaches that all that is infinite is God with mind, and that Antisthenes says there are many popular gods but one natural and principal God; and that Zeuxippus knows God as the natural, animating force by which all things are governed. What of Democritus? Although he first invented atoms, does he not often speak of nature, which generates images, and of intelligence, as God? Strato too says nature is God, and even Epicurus, who either imagines gods as idle or nonexistent, nevertheless sets nature above them. Aristotle varies, yet still assigns a single power: sometimes he calls mind God, sometimes the world, sometimes he places God over the world. Aristotle of Pontus varies, attributing the first principle now to the world, now to the divine mind. Heraclides of Pontus also ascribes the divine mind to God, though in varied ways. Theophrastus, Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes are likewise multiform, but all revolve around the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discusses God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as ether, most often as reason. Zeno, his teacher, holds that natural and divine law, and sometimes ether, sometimes reason, is the principle of all things. Likewise, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, fire as Vulcan, and showing that the other popular gods are elements, he seriously indicts and refutes the public error. Chrysippus is much the same, believing that divine power, rational nature, the world, and fatal necessity are God, and he imitates Zeno in the physiological interpretation of the songs of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus.

The Babylonian Diogenes also teaches the exposition and discussion of Jupiter's birth and Minerva's origin, and that these and other such names are words, not gods. The Socratic Xenophon denies that the form of the true God can be seen, and therefore should not be sought. The Stoic Aristo says God cannot be comprehended at all. Both sensed the majesty of God and despaired of understanding it. Plato's discourse on God, on things themselves, and on names is more open, and would be entirely heavenly if it were not sometimes sullied by the admixture of civil persuasion. Therefore in the Timaeus God is the Parent of the world, the artisan of the soul, the fabricator of heavenly and earthly things — difficult to find because of his excessive and incredible power, and impossible to speak of publicly once found. We hold almost the same things, for we know God and call him the Parent of all, and we never preach publicly unless we are asked.
